opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this question a lot, because Cosmos was never meant to be a model for its own sake. It's meant to be a platform that Physical AI developers build on. So the priorities really come from what those developers struggle with.

The first one, for me, is **physical accuracy**. A world model can generate a video that looks beautiful, but if the cup falls the wrong way, or the robot's hand passes through an object, that video is not just useless for training, it's harmful. It teaches the policy the wrong physics. So we need models that respect object permanence, contact, gravity, and the consistency of geometry over time. Visual quality was the first milestone. Physical correctness is the real one.

The second is **controllability**. Developers don't just want a plausible future. They want *the* future conditioned on a specific action, a specific camera trajectory, a specific change in the environment. If you're building an autonomous vehicle stack, you want to say, "Same intersection, but now it's raining at night and a pedestrian steps out." If you're doing robot manipulation, you want the world model to respond faithfully to the action the policy proposes. That action-conditioned behavior is what turns a video generator into a simulator you can actually use for policy evaluation and reinforcement learning.

The third is **long-horizon consistency**. Many physical tasks take minutes, not seconds. A model that drifts after a few seconds, where the kitchen layout quietly changes or an object disappears, can't support long tasks. So memory and spatial consistency over long rollouts are very important.

Fourth, **reasoning**. This is why we also built Cosmos Reason. A physical AI system needs to understand what is happening and what is likely to happen next, not only render pixels. Can the model tell you whether an action is safe, whether a generated clip violates physics, what the intention of an agent in the scene is? That kind of common-sense physical reasoning is useful both as a critic for generated data and as a component inside the robot's own decision making.

And finally, very practically, **efficiency and openness**. Developers need to post-train these models on their own robots, their own cameras, their own domains. If it takes a giant cluster just to fine-tune or run inference, adoption is limited. So we care about making the models smaller and faster to distill, providing good tokenizers, and keeping the weights and data pipelines open so people can adapt them.

If I had to summarize: the goal is for a developer to treat Cosmos as a reliable, controllable, physically faithful digital twin of the world, one that's cheap enough to run millions of times. That's what closes the data gap for Physical AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about what Cosmos should prioritize going forward, I keep coming back to the fact that Physical AI developers have a very different problem than people building chatbots. They don't have the internet as a training set. Every robot, every autonomous vehicle, every warehouse has its own embodiment, its own sensors, its own distribution of situations, and the rare cases that matter most are exactly the ones you can't collect enough of in the real world. So the first priority has to be world models that generalize across embodiments and can generate physically grounded data for the long tail. Not just visually plausible video, but video that respects contact, friction, deformation, lighting, the way objects actually behave when a gripper pushes them.

The second priority is controllability. A developer doesn't want a random sample of the world. They want to say, give me this scene at night, in rain, with a pedestrian stepping out from behind a truck, from the perspective of this specific camera rig. Conditioning on text, on trajectories, on depth, on segmentation, on the robot's own action stream, that's what makes the model useful as an engineering tool rather than a demo.

Third, I think the model has to become a reasoning engine, not only a generator. If the world model can predict what happens next given an action, then it can be used to evaluate policies, to plan, to tell you that a motion is going to fail before you execute it on hardware. That closes the loop between simulation and the real robot in a way that saves enormous amounts of time and broken equipment.

And finally, speed and openness. Physical AI runs on constrained compute, and it runs in a lot of different places. We need these models to be efficient enough to run in a tight loop, and open enough that developers can post-train them on their own data, because the real value shows up when a team fine-tunes a general world model into one that knows their factory floor better than anyone. That's the direction I want Cosmos to go: a foundation that the whole ecosystem can build their own physical intelligence on top of.

astra-6.text:
I think the priority should be helping Physical AI developers move from generating interesting videos to generating useful experience for their systems. That means better physical consistency: how objects move, how they interact, and how the world changes when a robot takes an action.

Controllability is also very important. A developer should be able to specify a scene, an action, or a constraint, then explore different possible outcomes. Can you vary the lighting, the layout, or the behavior of nearby people while keeping the rest of the scenario consistent? That would make these models much more useful for training and testing.

And I would prioritize longer-horizon consistency and uncertainty. A plausible future is not necessarily the future that will happen. Developers need to understand where a model is reliable and where they still need validation in the real world. Ultimately, the measure of progress should be whether these models help build robots and autonomous systems that perform better outside the simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are three capabilities we should prioritize. First is controllability. Physical AI developers need to specify what happens in a scene—the actions of a robot, the motion of objects, or changes in the environment—and have the model follow those instructions while maintaining physical consistency.

Second is the ability to predict how the world responds to an action. If a robot pushes an object or takes a particular path, what happens next? A useful world model should help developers explore those possibilities, including situations where the outcome is uncertain.

Third is making these capabilities practical: generating diverse training data, creating challenging scenarios for evaluation, and integrating with simulation and robotics workflows. Ultimately, the goal is to help developers build systems that behave reliably in the physical world.
